with_skill.expectation: Names gating decision-making information behind a login wall as a sales-enablement failure, not merely a content or UX shortcoming.

Checks whether each authoring persona - engineers pushing specs through CI/CD, business-side authors, technical writers as editors - has a workable workflow, instead of assuming one authoring workflow serves all of them.
Declines to commit a specific deflection percentage as a forecast in the business case.

without_skill.expectation: Names time to first call (TTFC) as the governing metric for this work and sets an explicit target figure for Ledgerwell.
Anchors that target to the API's complexity class - OAuth plus webhooks - landing near an hour rather than a sub-15-minute figure.
States that no universal TTFC benchmark exists, instead of presenting one number as an industry standard.
Recommends instrumenting TTFC in increments, at minimum landing-to-signup and signup-to-first-call, rather than as a single end-to-end number.
Explicitly demotes or defers role-and-use-case personalized onboarding intake, tying that to the six-week deadline and the part-time engineering capacity.
Any first-call acceleration figure attributed to a ready-to-run collection is expressed as a ratio of roughly 1.7x, labeled vendor-reported, with no baseline minute count carried over.
Warns that TTFC is a leading indicator only, and names downstream activation or retention as a trend to watch alongside it.
Declines to produce the requested plugin architecture and partner-facing navigation built on the internal service-catalog framework.
Gives the security reason: that framework's threat model assumes untrusted external actors have no access to it.
States that this option is ruled out entirely, not merely ranked lower, deferred, or made conditional on extra hardening.

Distinguishes an internal developer portal (service catalog, infrastructure provisioning for a company's own engineers) from an external API-consumer portal as different disciplines with different security models.
Names partner-specific requirements the external portal needs, including at least two of: approval-gated signup, team-owned applications, page-level visibility control, SSO/SCIM provisioning.
Presents at least two candidate portal architectures with trade-offs rather than a single structure, and names one as the recommendation.
States that the chosen skeleton will be validated with the user section by section before any final deliverable, rather than treating the structure as settled.
Recommends a structure layered by depth, with visual and marketing richness decreasing as pages get more technical.
Treats that solution layer as first-class rather than optional filler.
States that pricing, use cases and competitive/decision-making material must be readable before login.
Names gating decision-making information behind a login wall as a sales-enablement failure, not merely a content or UX shortcoming.
Keeps marketing chrome off the technical reference and console pages.
Keeps the portal distinct from the top-of-funnel marketing site while linking the two in both directions, rather than folding portal content into the marketing site's IA.

Scores the portal along three named dimensions covering authoring-workflow quality (operational excellence), journey friction (developer experience), and intentional interface strategy (business alignment).
Places the portal on a three-stage progression running portal-as-a-project, portal-as-a-product, portal-as-critical-business-infrastructure.
Refuses to reduce the assessment to a single maturity score or a fixed 1-to-5 level, and says why.
Delivers the output as a prioritized Priority 1 / Priority 2 / Priority 3 roadmap.
Runs a focus-area diagnostic spanning discovery, decision-making, onboarding, go-live, maintenance and troubleshooting, and community.

Checks whether each authoring persona - engineers pushing specs through CI/CD, business-side authors, technical writers as editors - has a workable workflow, instead of assuming one authoring workflow serves all of them.
Describes the benchmarking framework's structure rather than inventing a numeric scoring formula or enabler weightings for it.
States that the default recommendation is buying a managed platform - a gateway-bundled portal or a hosted docs/portal product - rather than building.
States the ranking across the options explicitly as a value, effort and efficiency ordering instead of leaving it implied by the order of discussion.
Rejects branding and pixel-level control on its own as a sufficient reason to promote a custom build.

Names the full set of custom-build promotion conditions: compliance or data-residency requirements no managed platform meets, business-side authors needing a real CMS alongside spec-driven docs, and a multi-gateway API portfolio no single vendor portal unifies.
Points out that Halcyon runs a single gateway across all products, so that gateway's bundled portal comes nearly free and the multi-gateway argument does not apply here.
Names the assembled-stack middle option: a docs platform for content composed with the gateway for credentials under one navigation.
Frames the decision by platform category rather than resolving it to one specific named vendor product.
Declines to commit a specific deflection percentage as a forecast in the business case.
States that published deflection figures around the 20-40% range are vendor-reported and directional only.
Requires measuring against Verdanta's own pre-assistant ticket baseline before claiming ROI, and recommends capturing that baseline before launch.
Keeps the existing classic full-text or semantic search rather than replacing it with the assistant.
Co-locates the Ask AI widget with the search box.
Treats support-ticket deflection as a watched trend rather than a gate the project passes or fails on.
Proposes a two-level hierarchy of organization to project (or workspace).
Scopes credentials, usage and environments to the project or workspace level rather than to the account or organization level.
Makes the environment marker visible on log and usage surfaces, not only on the credential list.
Adds partner-side controls beyond the public tier, including at least one of: team-owned or team-shared applications, page-level visibility permissions, a viewer-versus-consumer role split.
Raises the one-portal-versus-two question explicitly for the public and partner audiences, noting separate portals can share one API backend.
Frames that separate-portal question as an architectural decision rather than a licensing or vendor-packaging one.

Puts the try-it console on the endpoint page itself rather than as a separate tool the developer leaves the docs to open, with the signed-in developer's own key injected into it and into the code snippets.
Requires the API reference to be generated from the spec rather than hand-maintained as a parallel copy that drifts.
Scopes its own answer to placement, entry points and navigation, deferring the internal content design of individual surfaces rather than specifying it here.
